before.title: Deploy your WAF policy for Front Door in 'Prevention' mode.

queries.arg: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/frontdoorwebapplicationfirewallpolicies' | project policyName=name, policyId=id,policySku=sku.name, links=properties.securityPolicyLinks, enabledState=properties.policySettings.enabledState, mode=properties.policySettings.mode | mvexpand links | extend securityPolicy=links.id | extend securityPolicyParts=split(securityPolicy, '/') | extend profileId=strcat_array(array_slice(securityPolicyParts, 0, -3), '/') | project id=profileId, compliant=((enabledState=='Enabled') and (mode=='Prevention')), enabledState, mode

before.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorFrontEnds
before.title: Block common threats at the edge. WAF is integrated with Azure Front Door. Enable WAF rules on the front ends to protect applications from common exploits and vulnerabilities at the network edge, closer to the attack source.

before.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorRoleBasedAccessControlControlPlane
before.title: Allow only authorized access to the control plane. Use Azure Front Door role-based access control (RBAC) to restrict access to only the identities that need it.

before.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorSecurityBaseline
before.title: Review the security baseline for Azure Front Door.

before.name: wafsg-BackEndServersFrontEnd
before.title: Protect the back-end servers. The front end acts as the single point of ingress to the application.

before.name: wafsg-CentralizedSecurityInformationAnomalousActivity
before.title: Monitor anomalous activity. Regularly review the logs to check for attacks and false positives. Send WAF logs from Azure Front Door to your organization's centralized security information and event management (SIEM), such as Microsoft Sentinel, to detect threat patterns and incorporate preventative measures in the workload design.

before.name: wafsg-EndTransportLayerSecurityAzureFrontDoor
before.title: Protect data in transit. Enable end-to-end Transport Layer Security (TLS), HTTP to HTTPS redirection, and managed TLS certificates when applicable. For more information, see TLS best practices for Azure Front Door.

before.name: wafsg-FrontDoorCustomDomainEndpointsAzureFrontDoorManagedCertificates
before.title: Enable end-to-end TLS, HTTP to HTTPS redirection, and managed TLS certificates when applicable.  Review the TLS best practices for Azure Front Door.  Use TLS version 1.2 as the minimum allowed version with ciphers that are relevant for your application.  Azure Front Door managed certificates should be your default choice for ease of operations. However, if you want to manage the lifecycle of the certificates, use your own certificates in Azure Front Door custom domain endpoints and store them in Key Vault.
before.description: TLS ensures that data exchanges between the browser, Azure Front Door, and the back-end origins are encrypted to prevent tampering.  Key Vault offers managed certificate support and simple certificate renewal and rotation.

before.name: wafsg-OtherPublicIpAddressesDdosProtectionStandardPlan
before.title: Protect Azure Front Door against unexpected traffic. Azure Front Door uses the basic plan of Azure DDoS protection to protect application endpoints from DDoS attacks. If you need to expose other public IP addresses from your application, consider adding the DDoS Protection standard plan for those addresses for advanced protection and detection capabilities.

before.name: wafsg-OwaspTopAttackTypesMicrosoftThreatIntelligence
before.title: Enable WAF rule sets that detect and block potentially malicious traffic. This feature is available on the Premium tier. We recommend these rule sets:  - Default- Bot protection- IP restriction- Geo-filtering- Rate limiting
before.description: Default rule sets are updated frequently based on OWASP top-10 attack types and information from Microsoft Threat Intelligence.  The specialized rule sets detect certain use cases. For example, bot rules classify bots as good, bad, or unknown based on the client IP addresses. They also block bad bots and known IP addresses and restrict traffic based on geographical location of the callers.  By using a combination of rule sets, you can detect and block attacks with various intents.

before.name: wafsg-RuleSetsWafPolicy
before.title: Create exclusions for managed rule sets.  Test a WAF policy in detection mode for a few weeks and adjust any false positives before you deploy it.
before.description: Reduce false positives and allow legitimate requests for your application.

before.name: revcl-AzureFrontDoorAzureApplicationGateway
before.title: When using Azure Front Door and Azure Application Gateway to help protect HTTP/S apps, use WAF policies in Azure Front Door. Lock down Azure Application Gateway to receive traffic only from Azure Front Door.

before.name: revcl-InboundHttpSConnectionsAzureFrontDoor
before.title: Use Azure Front Door and WAF policies to provide global protection across Azure regions for inbound HTTP/S connections to a landing zone.

before.name: revcl-OtherReverseProxiesLandingZoneVirtualNetwork
before.title: Deploy WAFs and other reverse proxies are required for inbound HTTP/S connections, deploy them within a landing-zone virtual network and together with the apps that they're protecting and exposing to the internet.

before.name: revcl-AzureLoadBalancersStandardSku
before.title: Ensure you are using the Standard SKU for your Azure Load Balancers

queries.arg: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/loadbalancers' | project id, compliant=(tolower(sku.name) == 'standard')

before.name: revcl-LoadBalancersFrontendIpAddressesZonalFrontends
before.title: Ensure your Load Balancers frontend IP addresses are zone-redundant (unless you require zonal frontends).

before.name: revcl-ApplicationSecurityGroupsApplicationTeam
before.title: The application team should use application security groups at the subnet-level NSGs to help protect multi-tier VMs within the landing zone.

queries.arg: Resources | where type=='microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | project id,resourceGroup,name,subnets=properties.subnets | mv-expand subnets | project id,name,subnetName=subnets.name,subnetNsg=subnets.properties.networkSecurityGroup | where not (subnetName in ('GatewaySubnet', 'AzureFirewallSubnet', 'RouteServerSubnet', 'AzureBastionSubnet')) | extend compliant = isnotnull(subnetNsg)

before.name: revcl-ApplicationSecurityGroupsMicroSegmentTraffic
before.title: Use NSGs and application security groups to micro-segment traffic within the landing zone and avoid using a central NVA to filter traffic flows.

before.name: revcl-LandingZonesEastWestTraffic
before.title: Use NSGs to help protect traffic across subnets, as well as east/west traffic across the platform (traffic between landing zones).

before.name: revcl-NsgInboundDefaultRulesVirtualnetworkServiceTag
before.title: Don't rely on the NSG inbound default rules using the VirtualNetwork service tag to limit connectivity.

queries.arg: resources | where type=='microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | mvexpand properties.securityRules | project id,name,ruleAction=properties_securityRules.properties.access,rulePriority=properties_securityRules.properties.priority,ruleDst=properties_securityRules.properties.destinationAddressPrefix,ruleSrc=properties_securityRules.properties.sourceAddressPrefix,ruleProt=properties_securityRules.properties.protocol,ruleDirection=properties_securityRules.properties.direction,rulePort=properties_securityRules.properties.destinationPortRange | summarize StarDenies=countif(ruleAction=='Deny' and ruleDst=='*' and ruleSrc=='*' and ruleProt=='*' and rulePort=='*') by id,tostring(ruleDirection) | where ruleDirection == 'Inbound' | project id,compliant=(StarDenies>0) | union (resources | where type=='microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | where array_length(properties.securityRules)==0 | extend compliant=false | project id,compliant)

before.name: revcl-VnetFlowLogsExternalTrafficFlows
before.title: Enable VNet Flow Logs and feed them into Traffic Analytics to gain insights into internal and external traffic flows.

before.name: revcl-RouteServerSubnet
before.title: If using Route Server, use a /27 prefix for the Route Server subnet.

queries.arg: resources | where type=='microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | project id,subnets=properties.subnets | mv-expand subnets | project id, subnetName = subnets.name, subnetPrefix = subnets.properties.addressPrefix | extend subnetPrefixLength = split(subnetPrefix, '/')[1] | where subnetName == 'RouteServerSubnet' | extend compliant = (subnetPrefixLength <= 27) | distinct id, compliant

before.name: revcl-AddressAllocationRangesIpAddresses
before.title: Use IP addresses from the address allocation ranges for private internets (RFC 1918).

queries.arg: resources | where type == 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | extend addressSpace = todynamic(properties.addressSpace) | extend addressPrefix = todynamic(properties.addressSpace.addressPrefixes) | mvexpand addressSpace | mvexpand addressPrefix | project name, id, location, resourceGroup, subscriptionId, cidr = addressPrefix | extend compliant = (cidr matches regex @'^(10\\.|172\\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\\.|192\\.168\\.)')  | project id, compliant, cidr

before.name: revcl-DdosRelatedLogsPublicIpAddresses
before.title: Add diagnostic settings to save DDoS related logs for all the protected public IP addresses (DDoS IP or Network Protection).

before.name: revcl-IpProtectionPlansPublicIpAddresses
before.title: Use a DDoS Network or IP protection plans for all Public IP addresses in application landing zones.

before.name: revcl-PublicIpAddressesEndpointsIpProtectionPlans
before.title: Use Azure DDoS Network or IP Protection plans to help protect Public IP Addresses endpoints within the virtual networks.

before.name: revcl-SpokeNetworkTopologyNetworkDesign
before.title: Leverage a network design based on the traditional hub-and-spoke network topology for network scenarios that require maximum flexibility.

before.name: revcl-VirtualNetworkServiceEndpointsDefault
before.title: Don't enable virtual network service endpoints by default on all subnets.

queries.arg: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/virtualnetworks' | project id,resourceGroup,name,subnets = properties.subnets | mv-expand subnets | project id = subnets.id, resourceGroup, VNet = name, serviceEndpoints = subnets.properties.serviceEndpoints, compliant = (isnull(subnets.properties.serviceEndpoints) or array_length(subnets.properties.serviceEndpoints) == 0) | order by compliant asc

before.name: revcl-OutboundInternetTrafficProtectionAzureFirewall
before.title: For outbound Internet traffic protection and filtering, deploy Azure Firewall in secured hubs

queries.arg: resources | where type=='microsoft.network/virtualhubs' | extend compliant = isnotnull(properties.azureFirewall.id) | project id, compliant

before.name: revcl-AServiceBusClientAppServiceBusMessagingNamespace
before.title: When possible, your application should be using a managed identity to authenticate to Azure Service Bus. If not, consider having the storage credential (SAS, service principal credential) in Azure Key Vault or an equivalent service
before.description: A Service Bus client app running inside an Azure App Service application or in a virtual machine with enabled managed entities for Azure resources support does not need to handle SAS rules and keys, or any other access tokens. The client app only needs the endpoint address of the Service Bus Messaging namespace.

before.name: revcl-AzureServiceBusNamespaceClasslessInterDomainRoutingNotation
before.title: Consider only allowing access to Azure Service Bus namespace from specific IP addresses or ranges
before.description: With IP firewall, you can restrict the public endpoint further to only a set of IPv4 addresses or IPv4 address ranges in CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation.

before.name: revcl-AzureServiceBusNamespacesTransportLayerSecurity
before.title: Enforce a minimum required version of Transport Layer Security (TLS) for requests
before.description: Communication between a client application and an Azure Service Bus namespace is encrypted using Transport Layer Security (TLS). Azure Service Bus namespaces permit clients to send and receive data with TLS 1.0 and above. To enforce stricter security measures, you can configure your Service Bus namespace to require that clients send and receive data with a newer version of TLS.

before.name: revcl-AzureServiceBusPremiumCustomerManagedKeyOption
before.title: Use customer-managed key option in data at rest encryption when required
before.description: Azure Service Bus Premium provides encryption of data at rest. If you use your own key, the data is still encrypted using the Microsoft-managed key, but in addition the Microsoft-managed key will be encrypted using the customer-managed key.

before.name: revcl-AzureServiceBusPublicIpAddress
before.title: Consider using private endpoints to access Azure Service Bus and disable public network access when applicable.
before.description: Azure Service Bus by default has a public IP address and is Internet-reachable. Private endpoints allow traffic between your virtual network and Azure Service Bus traverses over the Microsoft backbone network. In addition to that, you should disable public endpoints if those are not used.

before.name: revcl-LeastPrivilegeDataPlaneRbacAzureServiceBus
before.title: Use least privilege data plane RBAC
before.description: When creating permissions, provide fine-grained control over a client's access to Azure Service Bus. Permissions in Azure Service Bus can and should be scoped to the individual resource level e.g. queue, topic or subscription.

before.name: revcl-ServiceBusNamespaceAdministrativeRootAccount
before.title: Avoid using root account when it is not necessary
before.description: When you create a Service Bus namespace, a SAS rule named RootManageSharedAccessKey is automatically created for the namespace. This policy has Manage permissions for the entire namespace. It's recommended that you treat this rule like an administrative root account and don't use it in your application.  Using AAD as an authentication provider with RBAC is recommended.

before.name: revcl-VariousDataPlaneAccessOperationsAzureServiceBusResourceLogs
before.title: Enable logging for security investigation. Use Azure Monitor to trace resource logs and runtime audit logs (currently available only in the premium tier)
before.description: Azure Service Bus resource logs include operational logs,  virtual network and IP filtering logs. Runtime audit logs capture aggregated diagnostic information for various data plane access operations (such as send or receive messages) in Service Bus.

before.name: revcl-AccidentalDeleteOperationSoftDelete
before.title: Enable 'soft delete' for containers
before.description: Soft delete for containers enables you to recover a container after it has been deleted, for example recover from an accidental delete operation.

before.name: revcl-AdHocSasServiceSasNearTermExpirationTimes
before.title: Strive for short validity periods for ad-hoc SAS
before.description: Use near-term expiration times on an ad hoc SAS service SAS or account SAS. In this way, even if a SAS is compromised, it's valid only for a short time. This practice is especially important if you cannot reference a stored access policy. Near-term expiration times also limit the amount of data that can be written to a blob by limiting the time available to upload to it.

before.name: revcl-ASasExpirationPolicySasExpirationPolicies
before.title: Consider configuring an SAS expiration policy
before.description: A SAS expiration policy specifies a recommended interval over which the SAS is valid. SAS expiration policies apply to a service SAS or an account SAS. When a user generates service SAS or an account SAS with a validity interval that is larger than the recommended interval, they'll see a warning.

before.name: revcl-AzureActiveDirectoryAzureAdTokens
before.title: Use Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tokens for blob access
before.description: AAD tokens should be favored over shared access signatures, wherever possible

before.name: revcl-AzureActiveDirectoryUserDelegationSas
before.title: When using SAS, prefer 'user delegation SAS' over storage-account-key based SAS.
before.description: A user delegation SAS is secured with Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) credentials and also by the permissions specified for the SAS. A user delegation SAS is analogous to a service SAS in terms of its scope and function, but offers security benefits over the service SAS.

before.name: revcl-ClassicDeploymentModelArmDeploymentModel
before.title: Ensure older storage accounts are not using 'classic deployment model'
before.description: Newly created storage accounts are created using the ARM deployment model, so that RBAC, auditing etc. are all enabled. Ensure that there are no old storage accounts with classic deployment model in a subscription

before.name: revcl-ClientSideEncryption
before.title: Determine which/if client-side encryption should be used.

before.name: revcl-ContainerSoftDeleteStorageAccount
before.title: Enable container soft delete for the storage account to recover a deleted container and its contents.

before.name: revcl-ControlPlaneOperationsActivityLogData
before.title: Consider using Azure Monitor to audit control plane operations on the storage account
before.description: Use Activity Log data to identify 'when', 'who', 'what' and 'how' the security of your storage account is being viewed or changed (i.e. storage account keys, access policies, etc.).

before.name: revcl-CrossOriginResourceSharingBroadCorsPolicies
before.title: Avoid overly broad CORS policies
before.description: Storage supports CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), i.e. an HTTP feature that enables web apps from a different domain to loosen the same-origin policy. When enabling CORS, keep the CorsRules to the least privilege.

before.name: revcl-CustomDomainsStorageAccount
before.title: When enforcing HTTPS (disabling HTTP), check that you do not use custom domains (CNAME) for the storage account.
before.description: When configuring a custom domain (hostname) on a storage account, check whether you need TLS/HTTPS; if so, you might have to put Azure CDN in front of your storage account.

before.name: revcl-KeyExpirationPolicyStorageAccountKeys
before.title: When using storage account keys, consider enabling a 'key expiration policy'
before.description: A key expiration policy enables you to set a reminder for the rotation of the account access keys. The reminder is displayed if the specified interval has elapsed and the keys have not yet been rotated.

before.name: revcl-LeastPrivilegeSecurityPrincipal
before.title: Least privilege in IaM permissions
before.description: When assigning a role to a user, group, or application, grant that security principal only those permissions that are necessary for them to perform their tasks. Limiting access to resources helps prevent both unintentional and malicious misuse of your data.

before.name: revcl-LeverageMicrosoftDefenderStorageAccounts
before.title: Enable Microsoft Defender for all of your storage accounts
before.description: Leverage Microsoft Defender to learn about suspicious activity and misconfigurations.

before.name: revcl-LeverageResourceGraphExplorerPublicBlobAccess
before.title: Consider whether public blob access is needed, or whether it can be disabled for certain storage accounts.
before.description: Leverage Resource Graph Explorer (resources | where type == 'microsoft.storage/storageaccounts' | where properties['allowBlobPublicAccess'] == true) to find storage accounts which allow anonymous blob access.

before.name: revcl-LittleAuditCapabilitiesUserDelegationSas
before.title: Consider disabling storage account keys, so that only AAD access (and user delegation SAS) is supported.
before.description: Storage account keys ('shared keys') have very little audit capabilities. While it can be monitored on who/when fetched a copy of the keys, once the keys are in the hands of multiple people, it is impossible to attribute usage to a specific user. Solely relying on AAD authentication makes it easier to tie storage access to a user.

before.name: revcl-MicrosoftCloudSecurityBenchmarkAzureSecurityBaseline
before.title: Consider the 'Azure security baseline for storage'
before.description: Apply guidance from the Microsoft cloud security benchmark related to Storage

before.name: revcl-NarrowScopeSingleResource
before.title: Apply a narrow scope to a SAS
before.description: When creating a SAS, be as specific and restrictive as possible. Prefer a SAS for a single resource and operation over a SAS which gives much broader access.

before.name: revcl-PlatformEncryption
before.title: Determine which/if platform encryption should be used.

before.name: revcl-PricingModelLargeContents
before.title: Consider checking uploaded data, after clients used a SAS to upload a file.
before.description: A SAS cannot constrain how much data a client uploads; given the pricing model of amount of storage over time, it might make sense to validate whether clients uploaded maliciously large contents.

before.name: revcl-PublicIpAddressAzureComputeResources
before.title: Consider using private endpoints for Azure Storage
before.description: Azure Storage by default has a public IP address and is Internet-reachable. Private endpoints allow to securely expose Azure Storage only to those Azure Compute resources that need access, thus eliminating exposure to the public Internet

before.name: revcl-ResourceLocksStorageAccounts
before.title: Enable resource locks on storage accounts
before.description: Prevents accidental deletion of a storage account, by forcing the user to first remove the deletion lock, prior to deletion

before.name: revcl-SecureTransferStorageAccounts
before.title: Secure transfer to storage accounts should be enabled

before.name: revcl-SftpEndpointAcls
before.title: SFTP: The SFTP endpoint does not support POSIX-like ACLs.

before.name: revcl-SharedAccessSignatureSasTokens
before.title: Limit shared access signature (SAS) tokens to HTTPS connections only
before.description: Requiring HTTPS when a client uses a SAS token to access blob data helps to minimize the risk of credential loss.

before.name: revcl-SoftDeleteBlobContainers
before.title: Disable 'soft delete' for blobs
before.description: Consider selectively disabling 'soft delete' for certain blob containers, for example if the application must ensure that deleted information is immediately deleted, e.g. for confidentiality, privacy or compliance reasons.

before.name: revcl-SoftDeleteComplianceReasons
before.title: Disable 'soft delete' for containers
before.description: Consider selectively disabling 'soft delete' for certain blob containers, for example if the application must ensure that deleted information is immediately deleted, e.g. for confidentiality, privacy or compliance reasons.

before.name: revcl-SoftDeleteSoftDeleteMechanism
before.title: Enable 'soft delete' for blobs
before.description: The soft-delete mechanism allows to recover accidentally deleted blobs.

before.name: revcl-SourceCodeRepositoryStorageAccountKeys
before.title: Consider configuring your application's source code repository to detect checked-in connection strings and storage account keys.

before.name: revcl-SpecificClientIpAddressClientIpAddresses
before.title: Consider scoping SAS to a specific client IP address, wherever possible
before.description: A SAS can include parameters on which client IP addresses or address ranges are authorized to request a resource using the SAS.

before.name: revcl-StorageAccountKeyAzureStorage
before.title: Consider storing connection strings in Azure KeyVault (in scenarios where managed identities are not possible)
before.description: Ideally, your application should be using a managed identity to authenticate to Azure Storage. If that is not possible, consider having the storage credential (connection string, storage account key, SAS, service principal credential) in Azure KeyVault or an equivalent service.

before.name: revcl-StorageAccountKeysStoredAccessPolicies
before.title: Consider linking SAS to a stored access policy
before.description: Stored access policies give you the option to revoke permissions for a service SAS without having to regenerate the storage account keys.

before.name: revcl-ThreadModelPlatformManagedKey
before.title: Determine how data at rest should be encrypted. Understand the thread model for data.
before.description: Data at rest is always encrypted server-side, and in addition might be encrypted client-side as well. Server-side encryption might happen using a platform-managed key (default) or customer-managed key. Client-side encryption might happen by either having the client supply an encryption/decryption key on a per-blob basis to Azure storage, or by completely handling encryption on the client-side. thus not relying on Azure Storage at all for confidentiality guarantees.

before.name: revcl-TimeBasedRetentionPoliciesLegalHold
before.title: Consider immutable blobs
before.description: Consider 'legal hold' or 'time-based retention' policies for blobs, so that is is impossible to delete the blob, the container, or the storage account. Please note that 'impossible' actually means 'impossible'; once a storage account contains an immutable blob, the only way to 'get rid' of that storage account is by cancelling the Azure subscription.

before.name: revcl-UnprotectedHttpAccessStorageAccount
before.title: Require HTTPS, i.e. disable port 80 on the storage account
before.description: Consider disabling unprotected HTTP/80 access to the storage account, so that all data transfers are encrypted, integrity protected, and the server is authenticated.

before.name: revcl-UsualRbacControlsLocalUserAccount
before.title: SFTP: Limit the amount of 'local users' for SFTP access, and audit whether access is needed over time.
before.description: When accessing blob storage via SFTP using a 'local user account', the 'usual' RBAC controls do not apply. Blob access via NFS or REST might be more restrictive than SFTP access. Unfortunately, as of early 2023, local users are the only form of identity management that is currently supported for the SFTP endpoint

before.name: wafsg-AccessControlListsSecurityRequirements
before.title: Understand your organization's security requirements: NFS Azure file shares only support Linux clients that use the NFSv4.1 protocol, with support for most features from the 4.1 protocol specification. Some security features, such as Kerberos authentication, access control lists (ACLs), and encryption in transit, aren't supported.

before.name: wafsg-AccessSignatureTokensSensitiveInformation
before.title: Protect sensitive information: Protect sensitive information such as account keys and shared access signature tokens. While these forms of authorization are generally not recommended, you should make sure to rotate, expire, and store them securely.

before.name: wafsg-AccountKeyKeyVault
before.title: We recommend that you don't use an account key. If you must use account keys, then store them in Key Vault, and make sure that you regenerate them periodically.
before.description: Key Vault lets you retrieve keys at runtime, instead of saving them by using your application. Key Vault also makes it easy to rotate your keys without interruption to your applications. Rotating the account keys periodically reduces the risk of exposing your data to malicious attacks.

before.name: wafsg-AccountNetworkControlsStorageAccount
before.title: Use network controls to restrict ingress and egress traffic: Disable all public traffic to the storage account. Use account network controls to grant the minimal level of access required by users and applications. For more information, see How to approach network security for your storage account.

before.name: wafsg-AesKerberosTicketEncryptionSmbAzureFileShares
before.title: When possible, use identity-based authentication with AES-256 Kerberos ticket encryption to authorize access to SMB Azure file shares.
before.description: Use identity-based authentication to decrease the possibility of an attacker using a storage account key to access file shares.

before.name: wafsg-AnonymousReadAccessAnonymousAccessSetting
before.title: Disable anonymous read access to containers and blob.
before.description: When anonymous access is allowed for a storage account, a user that has the appropriate permissions can modify a container's anonymous access setting to enable anonymous access to the data in that container.

before.name: wafsg-AzureExpressrouteConnectionTcpPort
before.title: Open TCP port 445 outbound or set up a VPN gateway or Azure ExpressRoute connection for clients outside of Azure to access the file share.
before.description: SMB 3.x is an internet-safe protocol, but you might not have the ability to change organizational or ISP policies. You can use a VPN gateway or an ExpressRoute connection as an alternative option.

before.name: wafsg-AzureFileSharesTransactionHeavyFileShares
before.title: Detect threats: Enable Microsoft Defender for Storage to detect potentially harmful attempts to access or exploit your Azure file shares over SMB or FileREST protocols. Subscription administrators get email alerts with details of suspicious activity and recommendations about how to investigate and remediate threats. Defender for Storage doesn't support antivirus capabilities for Azure file shares. If you use Defender for Storage, transaction-heavy file shares incur significant costs, so consider opting out of Defender for Storage for specific storage accounts.

before.name: wafsg-AzureFilesInsecureProtocol
before.title: If you open port 445, be sure to disable SMBv1 on Windows and Linux clients. Azure Files doesn't support SMB 1, but you should still disable it on your clients.
before.description: SMB 1 is an outdated, inefficient, and insecure protocol. Disable it on clients to improve your security posture.

before.name: wafsg-AzureResourceManagerLockDataLoss
before.title: Apply an Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account.
before.description: Locking an account prevents it from being deleted and causing data loss.

before.name: wafsg-AzureResourceManagerLockMaliciousDeletion
before.title: Apply an Azure Resource Manager lock  on the storage account.
before.description: Lock the account to prevent accidental or malicious deletion of the storage account, which can cause data loss.

before.name: wafsg-AzureRoleBasedAccessControlMicrosoftEntraId
before.title: Authorize access by using Azure role-based access control (RBAC).
before.description: With RBAC, there are no passwords or keys that can be compromised. The security principal (user, group, managed identity, or service principal) is authenticated by Microsoft Entra ID to return an OAuth 2.0 token. The token is used to authorize a request against the Blob Storage service.

before.name: wafsg-AzureStorageEncryptionStorageAccount
before.title: Consider using your own encryption key to protect the data in your storage account. For more information, see Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption.
before.description: Customer-managed keys provide greater flexibility and control. For example, you can store encryption keys in Key Vault and automatically rotate them.

before.name: wafsg-MicrosoftDefenderSubscriptionAdministrators
before.title: Detect threats: Enable Microsoft Defender for Storage to detect threats. Security alerts are triggered when anomalies in activity occur. The alerts notify subscription administrators via email with details of suspicious activity and recommendations on how to investigate and remediate threats.

before.name: wafsg-MicrosoftEntraIdSuperiorSecurity
before.title: Authorize access without using passwords or keys: Microsoft Entra ID provides superior security and ease of use compared to shared keys and shared access signatures. Grant security principals only those permissions that are necessary for them to do their tasks.

before.name: wafsg-MinimumRequiredLevelNetworkControls
before.title: Consider using network controls to restrict ingress and egress traffic: You might be comfortable exposing your storage account to the public internet under certain conditions, like if you use identity-based authentication to grant access to file shares. But we recommend that you use network controls to grant the minimum required level of access to users and applications. For more information, see How to approach network security for your storage account.

before.name: wafsg-ModernCryptographicAlgorithmsStorageAccount
before.title: Configure your storage account so clients can send and receive data by using the minimum version of TLS 1.2.
before.description: TLS 1.2 is more secure and faster than TLS 1.0 and 1.1, which don't support modern cryptographic algorithms and cipher suites.

before.name: wafsg-NfsAzureFileSharePort
before.title: You must open port 2049 on the clients that you want to mount your NFS share to.
before.description: Open port 2049 to let clients communicate with the NFS Azure file share.

before.name: wafsg-NfsAzureFileSharesNetworkLevelSecurity
before.title: Use network-level security and controls to restrict ingress and egress traffic: Identity-based authentication isn't available for NFS Azure file shares, so you must use network-level security and controls to grant the minimum required level of access to users and applications. For more information, see How to approach network security for your storage account.

before.name: wafsg-NonSecureHttpConnectionsTransportLayerSecurity
before.title: Reduce the attack surface: Preventing anonymous access, account key access, or access over non-secure (HTTP) connections can reduce the attack surface. Require clients to send and receive data by using the latest version of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

before.name: wafsg-OtherBusinessPurposesCriticalObjects
before.title: Protect critical objects: Apply immutability policies to protect critical objects. Policies protect blobs that are stored for legal, compliance, or other business purposes from being modified or deleted. Configure holds for set time periods or until restrictions are lifted by an administrator.

before.name: wafsg-RequireSecureTransferSettingStandardDataProcessingRates
before.title: NFS Azure file shares are only accessible through restricted networks. So you must create a private endpoint for your storage account or restrict public endpoint access to selected virtual networks and IP addresses. We recommend that you create a private endpoint. You must configure network-level security for NFS shares because Azure Files doesn't support encryption in transit with the NFS protocol. You need to disable the Require secure transfer setting on the storage account to use NFS Azure file shares. Standard data processing rates apply for private endpoints. If you don't require a static IP address for your file share and want to avoid the cost of private endpoints, you can restrict public endpoint access instead.
before.description: Network traffic travels over the Microsoft backbone network instead of the public internet, which eliminates risk exposure from the public internet.

before.name: wafsg-ResourceManagerLockMaliciousDeletion
before.title: Apply a Resource Manager lock on the storage account.
before.description: Lock the account to prevent accidental or malicious deletion of the storage account, which might cause data loss.

before.name: wafsg-SecureChannelEncryptionSmbProtocolVersion
before.title: Use only the most recent supported SMB protocol version (currently 3.1.1.), and use only AES-256-GCM for SMB channel encryption. Azure Files exposes settings that you can use to toggle the SMB protocol and make it more compatible or more secure, depending on your organization's requirements. By default, all SMB versions are allowed. However, SMB 2.1 is disallowed if you enable Require secure transfer because SMB 2.1 doesn't support encryption of data in transit. If you restrict these settings to a high level of security, some clients might not be able to connect to the file share.
before.description: SMB 3.1.1, released with Windows 10, contains important security and performance updates. AES-256-GCM offers more secure channel encryption.

before.name: wafsg-SecureTransferStorageAccounts
before.title: Enable the secure transfer required option: Enabling this setting for all your storage accounts ensures that all requests made against the storage account must take place over secure connections. Any requests made over HTTP fail.

before.name: wafsg-SecurityBaselineAzureStorage
before.title: Review the security baseline for Azure Storage: To get started, first review the security baseline for Storage.

before.name: wafsg-SharedAccessSignatureTokenAccessSignatureBestPractices
before.title: We recommend that you don't use shared access signature tokens. Evaluate whether you need shared access signature tokens to secure access to Blob Storage resources. If you must create one, then review this list of shared access signature best practices before you create and distribute it.
before.description: Best practices can help you prevent a shared access signature token from being leaked and quickly recover if a leak does occur.

before.name: wafsg-SharedKeyAuthorizationAccessSignatureTokens
before.title: Disallow shared key authorization. This disables not only account key access but also service and account shared access signature tokens because they're based on account keys.
before.description: Only secured requests that are authorized with Microsoft Entra ID are permitted.

before.name: wafsg-SmbFileSharesMostCases
before.title: In most cases, you should enable the Secure transfer required option on all your storage accounts to enable encryption in transit for SMB file shares. Don't enable this option if you need to allow very old clients to access the share. If you disable secure transfer, be sure to use network controls to restrict traffic.
before.description: This setting ensures that all requests that are made against the storage account take place over secure connections (HTTPS). Any requests made over HTTP will fail.

before.name: wafsg-SpecificVirtualNetworksFirewallRules
before.title: Enable firewall rules that limit access to specific virtual networks. Start with zero access, and then methodically and incrementally provide the least amount of access required for clients and services.
before.description: Minimize the risk of creating openings for attackers.

before.name: wafsg-SpecificVirtualNetworksPublicEndpoints
before.title: Disable traffic to the public endpoints of your storage account. Create private endpoints for clients that run in Azure. Enable the public endpoint only if clients and services external to Azure require direct access to your storage account. Enable firewall rules that limit access to specific virtual networks.
before.description: Start with zero access and then incrementally authorize the lowest levels of access required for clients and services to minimize the risk of creating unnecessary openings for attackers.

before.name: wafsg-StandardDataProcessingRatesSpecificVirtualNetworks
before.title: Consider disabling public network access to your storage account. Enable public network access only if SMB clients and services that are external to Azure require access to your storage account. If you disable public network access,create a private endpoint for your storage account. Standard data processing rates for private endpoints apply. A private endpoint doesn't block connections to the public endpoint. You should still disable public network access as previously described. If you don't require a static IP address for your file share and want to avoid the cost of private endpoints, you can instead restrict public endpoint access to specific virtual networks and IP addresses.
before.description: Network traffic travels over the Microsoft backbone network instead of the public internet, which eliminates risk exposure from the public internet.

before.name: wafsg-StorageAccountKeyAccessSmbSecuritySettings
before.title: If you use storage account keys, store them in Key Vault, and make sure to regenerate them periodically. You can completely disallow storage account key access to the file share by removing NTLMv2 from the share's SMB security settings. But you generally shouldn't remove NTLMv2 from the share's SMB security settings because administrators still need to use the account key for some tasks.
before.description: Use Key Vault to retrieve keys at runtime instead of saving them with your application. Key Vault also makes it easy to rotate your keys without interruption to your applications. Periodically rotate the account keys to reduce the risk of exposing your data to malicious attacks.

before.name: wafsg-StorageAccountKeyAccessStorageAccountLevel
before.title: Consider disallowing storage account key access at the storage account level. You don't need this access to mount NFS file shares. But keep in mind that full administrative control of a file share, including the ability to take ownership of a file, requires use of a storage account key.
before.description: Disallow the use of storage account keys to make your storage account more secure.

before.name: wafsg-StorageAccountKeysFullAdministrativeControl
before.title: Minimize the use of storage account keys: Identity-based authentication provides superior security compared to using a storage account key. But you must use a storage account key to get full administrative control of a file share, including the ability to take ownership of a file. Grant security principals only the necessary permissions that they need to perform their tasks.

before.name: wafsg-StorageAccountKeysSensitiveInformation
before.title: Protect sensitive information: Protect sensitive information, such as storage account keys and passwords. We don't recommend that you use these forms of authorization, but if you do, you should make sure to rotate, expire, and store them securely.

before.name: wafsg-TransportLayerSecurityTlsProtocolAttackSurface
before.title: Reduce the attack surface: Use encryption in transit and prevent access over non-secure (HTTP) connections to reduce the attack surface. Require clients to send and receive data by using the latest version of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

before.name: revcl-AppServiceAccessRestrictionsDifferentAccessRestrictions
before.title: Inbound network access should be controlled
before.description: Control inbound network access using a combination of App Service Access Restrictions, Service Endpoints or Private Endpoints. Different access restrictions can be required and configured for the web app itself and the SCM site.

before.name: revcl-AppServiceActivityLogsAppServiceResource
before.title: Send App Service activity logs to Log Analytics
before.description: Set up a diagnostic setting to send the activity log to Log Analytics as the central destination for logging and monitoring. This allows you to monitor control plane activity on the App Service resource itself.

before.name: revcl-AppServiceKeyVaultReferencesAzureKeyVault
before.title: Use Key Vault to store secrets
before.description: Use Azure Key Vault to store any secrets the application needs.  Key Vault provides a safe and audited environment for storing secrets and is well-integrated with App Service through the Key Vault SDK or App Service Key Vault References.

before.name: revcl-AppServiceKeyVaultReferencesKeyVaultSdk
before.title: Use Managed Identity to connect to Key Vault
before.description: Use a Managed Identity to connect to Key Vault either using the Key Vault SDK or through App Service Key Vault References.

before.name: revcl-AppServiceRuntimeLogsRuntimeActivity
before.title: Send App Service runtime logs to Log Analytics
before.description: By configuring the diagnostic settings of App Service, you can send all telemetry to Log Analytics as the central destination for logging and monitoring. This allows you to monitor runtime activity of App Service such as HTTP logs, application logs, platform logs, ...

before.name: revcl-AppServiceTlsCertificateKeyVault
before.title: Use Key Vault to store TLS certificate.
before.description: Store the App Service TLS certificate in Key Vault.

before.name: revcl-AuthenticatedWebApplicationAzureAdBC
before.title: Use an established Identity Provider for authentication
before.description: For authenticated web application, use a well established Identity Provider like Azure AD or Azure AD B2C.  Leverage the application framework of your choice to integrate with this provider or use the App Service Authentication / Authorization feature.

before.name: revcl-AzureAdCredentialsBasicAuthentication
before.title: Disable basic authentication
before.description: Disable basic authentication for both FTP/FTPS and for WebDeploy/SCM.  This disables access to these services and enforces the use of Azure AD secured endpoints for deployment.  Note that the SCM site can also be opened using Azure AD credentials.

before.name: revcl-AzureContainerRegistryManagedIdentity
before.title: Pull containers using a Managed Identity
before.description: Where using images stored in Azure Container Registry, pull these using a Managed Identity.

before.name: revcl-AzureContainerRegistryVirtualNetwork
before.title: Pull containers over a Virtual Network
before.description: Where using images stored in Azure Container Registry, pull these over a virtual network from Azure Container Registry using its private endpoint and the app setting 'WEBSITE_PULL_IMAGE_OVER_VNET'.

before.name: revcl-CorsConfigurationWildcards
before.title: Wildcards must not be used for CORS
before.description: Do not use wildcards in your CORS configuration, as this allows all origins to access the service (thereby defeating the purpose of CORS). Specifically only allow the origins that you expect to be able to access the service.

before.name: revcl-DevopsDeploymentPipelineTrustedEnvironment
before.title: Deploy from a trusted environment
before.description: Deploy code to App Service from a controlled and trusted environment, like a well-managed and secured DevOps deployment pipeline. This avoids code that was not version controlled and verified to be deployed from a malicious host.

before.name: revcl-HttpStrictTransportSecurityAppService
before.title: Use HTTPS only
before.description: Configure App Service to use HTTPS only.  This causes App Service to redirect from HTTP to HTTPS.  Strongly consider the use of HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) in your code or from your WAF, which informs browsers that the site should only be accessed using HTTPS.

queries.arg: where (type=='microsoft.web/sites' and (kind == 'app' or kind == 'app,linux' )) | extend compliant = (properties.httpsOnly==true) | distinct id,compliant

before.name: revcl-IntelligentDdosStandardCapabilitiesDdosProtectionStandard
before.title: Enable DDOS Protection Standard on the WAF VNet
before.description: Azure provides DDoS Basic protection on its network, which can be improved with intelligent DDoS Standard capabilities which learns about normal traffic patterns and can detect unusual behavior. DDoS Standard applies to a Virtual Network so it must be configured for the network resource in front of the app, such as Application Gateway or an NVA.

before.name: revcl-LatestVersionsDatePlatforms-1
before.title: Use up-to-date platforms, languages, protocols and frameworks
before.description: Use the latest versions of supported platforms, programming languages, protocols, and frameworks.

before.name: revcl-MaliciousInboundTrafficWebApplicationFirewall
before.title: Use a WAF in front of App Service
before.description: Protect against malicious inbound traffic using a Web Application Firewall like Application Gateway or Azure Front Door.  Make sure to monitor the WAF's logs.

before.name: revcl-MaliciousIpAddressesAppService
before.title: Enable Defender for Cloud - Defender for App Service
before.description: Enable Defender for App Service.  This (amongst other threats) detects communications to known malicious IP addresses.  Review the recommendations from Defender for App Service as part of your operations.

before.name: revcl-ManagedIdentityAzureAd
before.title: Use Managed Identity to connect to resources
before.description: Where possible use Managed Identity to connect to Azure AD secured resources.  If this is not possible, store secrets in Key Vault and connect to Key Vault using a Managed Identity instead.

before.name: revcl-MinimumTlsPolicyAppServiceConfiguration
before.title: Set minimum TLS policy to 1.2
before.description: Set minimum TLS policy to 1.2 in App Service configuration.

queries.arg: appserviceresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites/config' | extend compliant = (properties.MinTlsVersion>=1.2) | distinct id,compliant

before.name: revcl-OutboundNetworkAccessRegionalVnetIntegration
before.title: Outbound network access should be controlled
before.description: Control outbound network access using a combination of regional VNet integration, network security groups and UDR's.  Traffic should be routed to an NVA such as Azure Firewall.  Ensure to monitor the Firewall's logs.

before.name: revcl-PenetrationTestingRulesWebApplication
before.title: Conduct a penetration test
before.description: Conduct a penetration test on the web application following the penetration testing rules of engagement.

before.name: revcl-RemoteDebuggingAdditionalPorts
before.title: Turn off remote debugging
before.description: Remote debugging must not be turned on in production as this opens additional ports on the service which increases the attack surface. Note that the service does turn of remote debugging automatically after 48 hours.

queries.arg: appserviceresources | where type =~ 'microsoft.web/sites/config' | extend compliant = (properties.RemoteDebuggingEnabled == false) | distinct id,compliant

before.name: revcl-SensitiveDataLocalDisk
before.title: Do not store sensitive data on local disk
before.description: Local disks on App Service are not encrypted and sensitive data should not be stored on those.  (For example: D:\\Local and %TMP%).

before.name: revcl-SeparateAppServicePlansAppServiceEnvironments
before.title: Isolate systems that process sensitive information
before.description: Systems that process sensitive information should be isolated.  To do so, use separate App Service Plans or App Service Environments and consider the use of different subscriptions or management groups.

before.name: revcl-ServiceEndpointsPrivateEndpoints
before.title: Avoid for WAF to be bypassed
before.description: Make sure the WAF cannot be bypassed by locking down access to only the WAF.  Use a combination of Access Restrictions, Service Endpoints and Private Endpoints.

before.name: revcl-StableOutboundIpRangeVnetNatGateway
before.title: Ensure a stable IP for outbound communications towards internet addresses
before.description: You can provide a stable outbound IP by using VNet integration and using a VNet NAT Gateway or an NVA like Azure Firewall.  This allows the receiving party to allow-list based on IP, should that be needed.  Note that for communications towards Azure Services often there's no need to depend on the IP address and mechanics like Service Endpoints should be used instead.  (Also the use of private endpoints on the receiving end avoids for SNAT to happen and provides a stable outbound IP range.)

before.name: revcl-ValidatedCodeTrustedCode
before.title: Deploy validated code
before.description: Deploy trusted code that was validated and scanned for vulnerabilities according to DevSecOps practices.

before.name: wafsg-AppServiceAppsAzureVirtualNetwork
before.title: Create segmentation through isolation boundaries to contain breach: Apply identity segmentation. For example, implement role-based access control (RBAC) to assign specific permissions based on roles. Follow the principle of least privilege to limit access rights to only what's necessary. Also create segmentation at the network level. Inject App Service apps in an Azure virtual network for isolation and define network security groups (NSGs) to filter traffic.

before.name: wafsg-AppServicePlanSecurityBaselines
before.title: Review security baselines: To enhance the security posture of your application that's hosted on an App Service plan, review the security baseline for App Service.

before.name: wafsg-AppServiceWebApp
before.title: (App Service) Assign managed identities to the web app. To maintain isolation boundaries, don't share or reuse identities across applications.  Make sure that you securely connect to your container registry if you use containers for your deployment.
before.description: The application retrieves secrets from Key Vault to authenticate outward communication from the application. Azure manages the identity and doesn't require you to provision or rotate any secrets.  You have distinct identities for granularity of control. Distinct identities make revocation easy if an identity is compromised.

before.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorNetworkTraffic
before.title: Control network traffic to and from the application: Don't expose application endpoints to the public internet. Instead, add a private endpoint on the web app that's placed in a dedicated subnet. Front your application with a reverse proxy that communicates with that private endpoint. Consider using Application Gateway or Azure Front Door for that purpose.

before.name: wafsg-AzureKeyVaultReferencesSensitiveInformation
before.title: Protect application secrets: You need to handle sensitive information, like API keys or authentication tokens. Instead of hardcoding these secrets directly into your application code or configuration files, you can use Azure Key Vault references in app settings. When the application starts, App Service automatically retrieves the secret values from Key Vault by using the app's managed identity.

before.name: wafsg-AzureStorageAccountsAzureEventHubs
before.title: (App Service plan) Enable diagnostic logging and add instrumentation to your app. The logs are sent to Azure Storage accounts, Azure Event Hubs, and Log Analytics. For more information about audit log types, see Supported log types.
before.description: Logging captures access patterns. It records relevant events that provide valuable insights into how users interact with an application or platform. This information is crucial for accountability, compliance, and security purposes.

before.name: wafsg-ComprehensiveActivityTrailsResourceLogs
before.title: Enable resource logs for your application: Enable resource logs for your application to create comprehensive activity trails that provide valuable data during investigations that follow security incidents.

before.name: wafsg-KeyVaultReferencesSecretRotations
before.title: (App Service) Always use Key Vault references as app settings.
before.description: Secrets are kept separate from your app's configuration. App settings are encrypted at rest. App Service also manages secret rotations.

before.name: wafsg-LanguageRuntimeSupportPolicyLatestRuntime
before.title: Use the latest runtime and libraries: Thoroughly test your application builds before you do updates to catch problems early and ensure a smooth transition to the new version. App Service supports the language runtime support policy for updating existing stacks and retiring end-of-support stacks.

before.name: wafsg-MicrosoftEntraIdBasedAuthenticationSecureDeploymentMethod
before.title: (App Service) To implement hardening:  - Disable basic authentication that uses a username and password in favor of Microsoft Entra ID-based authentication.  - Turn off remote debugging so that inbound ports aren't opened. - Enable CORS policies to tighten incoming requests.  - Disable protocols, such as FTP.
before.description: We don't recommend basic authentication as a secure deployment method. Microsoft Entra ID employs OAuth 2.0 token-based authentication, which offers numerous advantages and enhancements that address the limitations that are associated with basic authentication.  Policies restrict access to application resources, only allow requests from specific domains, and secure cross-region requests.

before.name: wafsg-MicrosoftEntraIdMultipleSignInProviders
before.title: (App Service) valuate whether App Service built-in authentication is the right mechanism to authenticate users that access your application. App Service built-in authentication integrates with Microsoft Entra ID. This feature handles token validation and user identity management across multiple sign-in providers and supports OpenID Connect. With this feature, you don't have authorization at a granular level, and you don't have a mechanism to test authentication.
before.description: When you use this feature, you don't have to use authentication libraries in application code, which reduces complexity. The user is already authenticated when a request reaches the application.

before.name: wafsg-OverallSecurityPostureAccessControls
before.title: Apply access controls on identities: Restrict both inward access to the web app and outward access from the web app to other resources. This configuration applies access controls on identities and helps maintain the workload's overall security posture.

before.name: wafsg-OverallSecurityPostureAppServicePlan
before.title: (App Service plan) Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud for App Service.
before.description: Get real-time protection for resources that run in an App Service plan. Guard against threats and enhance your overall security posture.

before.name: wafsg-SourceControlManagerFileTransferProtocol
before.title: Reduce the attack surface: Remove default configurations that you don't need. For example, disable remote debugging, local authentication for Source Control Manager (SCM) sites, and basic authentication. Disable unsecure protocols like HTTP and File Transfer Protocol (FTP). Enforce configurations through Azure policies. For more information, see Azure policies.

before.name: wafsg-TransportLayerSecurityAppService
before.title: (App Service) Configure custom domains for applications.  Disable HTTP and only accept HTTPS requests.
before.description: Custom domains enable secure communication through HTTPS using Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, which ensures the protection of sensitive data and builds user trust.

before.name: wafsg-TransportLayerSecurityCustomerManagedKeys
before.title: Encrypt data: Protect data in transit with end-to-end Transport Layer Security (TLS). Use your customer-managed keys for full encryption of data at rest. For more information, see Encryption at rest using customer-managed keys.

before.name: wafsg-VirtualNetworkIntegrationAzureVirtualNetwork
before.title: (App Service) Configure the application for virtual network integration.  Use private endpoints for App Service apps. Block all public traffic.  Route the container image pull through the virtual network integration. All outgoing traffic from the application passes through the virtual network.
before.description: Get the security benefits of using an Azure virtual network. For example, the application can securely access resources within the network.   Add a private endpoint to help protect your application. Private endpoints limit direct exposure to the public network and allow controlled access through the reverse proxy.
